text: Hello, I am Dr. Agent. Can you describe the nature of his stools and whether he has experienced any vomiting or failure to thrive? Also, when was his first bowel movement after birth?

text: The baby has been very fussy, feeding less than usual, and the abdomen looks distended. Crying gets worse when the belly is touched.

speaker: Doctor
text: Did he pass meconium within the first 48 hours of life, and have you noticed any ribbon-like stools or explosive watery stools when the abdomen is examined?

speaker: Doctor
text: The normal anorectal manometry makes Hirschsprung's disease unlikely, so I suspect a mechanical obstruction like intestinal atresia or malrotation. Let's proceed with an upper GI series to evaluate for malrotation or atresia. REQUEST TEST: Upper GI Series.

speaker: Doctor
text: Given the distension, delayed meconium, and normal upper GI series, I suspect a lower intestinal obstruction such as ileal atresia or meconium ileus. I will request an abdominal ultrasound to look for target signs of intussusception or other structural anomalies. REQUEST TEST: Abdominal Ultrasound.

speaker: Doctor
text: Since the manometry is normal, Hirschsprung's is effectively ruled out. Given the abdominal distension and feeding difficulties in an 8-month-old, could you describe the specific consistency of his stools and whether he has had any episodes of projectile vomiting?

speaker: Patient
text: The baby did not seem to pass stool normally and the belly swelling has become more obvious. Feeding has clearly decreased over the past few days.

speaker: Doctor
text: Has there been any visible blood or mucus in his stools, and does the distension improve after passing gas or stool? I will REQUEST TEST: Contrast Enema to evaluate for intestinal atresia or strictures.
